# Abstract

The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve is a fundamental tool for evaluating the classification accuracy of continuous diagnostic tests. While the partial area under the ROC curve (pAUC) serves as a widely accepted summary measure offering generality and probabilistic interpretability, its extension to time-to-event data presents unique challenges in biomarker evaluation for disease detection over time. This paper proposes novel nonparametric estimators for time-dependent pAUC that feature closed-form expressions and computational efficiency without relying on trapezoidal approximation rules. We establish the asymptotic properties of these estimators as gaussian processes and derive explicit variance-covariance function estimates, facilitating the construction of valid confidence intervals for statistical inference. The finite-sample performance of the proposed methodology is comprehensively evaluated through extensive simulation studies, demonstrating robust behavior across various scenarios. We illustrate the practical utility of our approach by analyzing CD4 cell counts as predictors of survival time in the AIDS Clinical Trials Group (ACTG) 175 study. Furthermore, we extend the framework to enable comparative inference between time-dependent pAUCs across patient subgroups, specifically contrasting patients with and without prior antiretroviral therapy. The proposed methods provide researchers with accessible and statistically rigorous tools for evaluating time-dependent biomarker performance in clinical applications.

# Abstract

Astronomy has historically driven civilization's advancement through both conceptual frameworks and practical applications derived from celestial observations. In modern times, space sciences have served as the foundational engine for space technology development, fundamentally shaping contemporary society. However, current trends demonstrate a declining emphasis on science within space programs, prioritizing commercial and applications-driven approaches over fundamental research. This shift threatens societal autonomy in space-related matters that increasingly affect daily life on Earth. Reversing this trend is essential to ensure that modern societies maintain independent capabilities and decision-making authority in space sciences and technologies, preserving the scientific foundation necessary for continued innovation and self-determination in an era where space-based systems are integral to global communication, navigation, and resource management.

We investigate the origin of large-scale cosmic ray anisotropy observed at TeV energies through a modified Compton-Getting effect in magnetized flows from aged supernova remnants. Our model identifies an optimal energy scale for anisotropy detection and relies on two fundamental assumptions: cosmic ray propagation governed by Kolmogorov turbulence and particle transport dominated by stellar winds from progenitor stars. The framework predicts characteristic energy-dependent behavior: reduced anisotropy amplitude at lower energies resulting from incomplete velocity field sampling, and suppression at higher energies due to enhanced diffusive smearing. This interpretation provides a self-consistent explanation for the observed @xmath0 TeV anisotropy and offers testable predictions for multi-energy observations of cosmic ray arrival directions.

# Abstract

We propose a novel approach to image segmentation based on the eigenvalue problem of an anisotropic diffusion operator, where the diffusion matrix is constructed adaptively from features of the input image. The eigenfunctions of this operator and the projection of the input image onto selected eigenspaces effectively capture essential structural information and salient features present in the image. A particularly advantageous property of our model is that, for a broad class of input images, the leading eigenfunctions exhibit piecewise constant behavior, making them naturally suited for image segmentation, edge detection, and related vision tasks.

We establish theoretical connections between our continuous eigenvalue formulation and the algebraic eigenvalue problems arising in discrete spectral clustering methods commonly employed in image analysis. This relationship provides deeper theoretical insight into spectral segmentation algorithms and facilitates the development of more efficient numerical implementations with rigorous mathematical foundations. Unlike energy-minimization approaches such as geodesic active contours, our method requires no initial guess or manual initialization, enhancing its robustness and ease of use. Furthermore, the multi-scale characteristics emerge naturally from the anisotropic diffusion operator itself, eliminating the need for solving eigenvalue problems across multiple resolution levels.

For numerical implementation, we develop a finite element scheme incorporating an adaptive mesh refinement strategy specifically designed for anisotropic structures. Our computational experiments demonstrate that this adaptive approach yields significantly more accurate eigenfunctions compared to uniform mesh discretizations. Through extensive numerical examples, we examine several interesting theoretical and practical features of the proposed model, including its behavior on various image types, computational efficiency, and potential applications in computer vision and image processing tasks.

# Abstract

We investigate the magnetic properties of isolated mesoscopic metallic grains, demonstrating that electron-electron interactions can be effectively described by a simple interaction Hamiltonian containing only three coupling constants: charging energy, exchange interaction, and superconducting pairing. This universal description requires large Thouless conductance, ensuring negligible sample-to-sample fluctuations in coupling constants. Nevertheless, thermodynamic properties remain sample-specific due to mesoscopic fluctuations in the single-particle spectrum.

For grains composed of materials near the ferromagnetic instability threshold, we find dramatically enhanced mesoscopic magnetization fluctuations. The system exhibits multi-stability, where the free energy landscape as a function of magnetization develops numerous local minima. We develop a statistical theory for characterizing these minima and establish universal scaling properties governing their distribution. These scaling laws describe how the density and depth of metastable states depend on system parameters and grain size.

Our numerical simulations confirm the predicted scaling behavior and reveal the complex energy landscape characteristic of mesoscopic Stoner instability. This work provides a framework for understanding magnetic bistability and sample-specific magnetic properties in nanoscale ferromagnetic systems, with implications for magnetic memory applications and quantum dot magnetism.

# Abstract

We investigate the non-perturbative properties of N=1 supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory through numerical lattice simulations, focusing on the spectrum of bound states and the emergence of supersymmetry in the continuum limit. Using improved lattice techniques at fine lattice spacing, we compute the masses of key particles including the gluino-glue state, mesonic states, and scalar glueballs with unprecedented statistical precision and enhanced control over systematic effects such as finite volume artifacts and lattice discretization errors. Our results represent a significant advancement over previous lattice studies in terms of both statistical accuracy and systematic uncertainty control. Within the combined statistical and systematic error bars of our calculations, we observe that the masses of fermionic and bosonic bound states are compatible with forming degenerate supermultiplets, as required by unbroken supersymmetry. This mass degeneracy provides strong evidence that supersymmetry is preserved in the continuum limit without spontaneous breaking, contradicting earlier lattice investigations that suggested possible supersymmetry breaking. These findings have important implications for understanding the non-perturbative dynamics of supersymmetric gauge theories and their potential role in physics beyond the Standard Model.

We investigate the Klein-Gordon (KG) equation through a five-dimensional space-time framework, demonstrating that this approach provides new insights into relativistic quantum mechanics. We explicitly show that the KG equation in flat space-time admits a consistent probabilistic interpretation with positively defined probability density, addressing long-standing concerns about negative probabilities. However, we find that this probabilistic interpretation lacks covariance under Lorentz transformations. In the non-relativistic limit, our formalism naturally reduces to the standard Schrödinger equation, ensuring consistency with non-relativistic quantum mechanics. The 5D perspective reveals alternative interpretations of the KG equation and their corresponding non-relativistic limits. As a concrete application, we apply our framework to analyze hydrogenic spectra and calculate the canonical partition function of the hydrogen atom. This five-dimensional approach offers a unified perspective bridging relativistic and non-relativistic quantum theory while clarifying foundational issues in the interpretation of the Klein-Gordon equation.

## Abstract

This paper presents a comprehensive review of the Very Large Array (VLA) 74 MHz system, developed through a collaboration between the Naval Research Laboratory and the National Radio Astronomy Observatory and commissioned in 1998. Operating at 73.8 MHz, this low-frequency capability represents a significant advance in radio astronomy, offering unprecedented sensitivity (approximately @xmath0) combined with angular resolutions ranging from 25" on standard VLA baselines to 12" when extended to include the Pie Town antenna of the Very Long Baseline Array.

The primary technical challenge at these frequencies stems from ionospheric phase fluctuations, which fundamentally influence observing strategies and data calibration approaches. We describe two distinct calibration methodologies developed to address varying ionospheric conditions. The first, an **angle-invariant calibration strategy**, applies when observing restricted fields of view or during periods of exceptionally quiescent ionospheric conditions—specifically when the ionospheric isoplanatic patch size exceeds the field of view. This approach employs a single phase correction per antenna, typically derived through self-calibration, analogous to techniques used at higher radio frequencies. The second, a **field-based calibration strategy**, becomes necessary for wider fields of view or more typical ionospheric conditions when the isoplanatic patch size is smaller than the observed field. This innovative approach models the ionosphere above the array using Zernike polynomials, allowing phase corrections to vary spatially across the field of view.

We present observational results demonstrating both calibration strategies. Images of moderately strong 3C catalog sources exemplify routine angle-invariant calibration and illustrate typical data quality. Flux density measurements of sources with well-established low-frequency spectra confirm that the VLA 74 MHz flux scale is stable to within a few percent, with absolute flux densities referenced to the Baars et al. value for Cygnus A reliable to at least 5%. Additionally, we present a wide-field image constructed using field-based calibration, demonstrating the detection of hundreds of weaker sources in fields without dominant bright objects.

Beyond calibration, we address other practical considerations unique to low-frequency observations, including radio frequency interference excision techniques and wide-field imaging methodologies that differ substantially from higher-frequency practice. The hardware implementation, system performance characteristics, and operational procedures are thoroughly documented.

This work provides both a practical guide for observers using the VLA 74 MHz system and a valuable reference for the design and operation of emerging low-frequency radio telescopes worldwide. The lessons learned from this system—particularly regarding ionospheric calibration strategies and wide-field imaging—offer important insights for next-generation instruments operating in this challenging but scientifically rich frequency regime.

# Abstract

We develop a coordinate space quasi-particle random phase approximation (QRPA) formalism, extending the RPA model of Shlomo and Bertsch to open-shell nuclei by incorporating pairing correlations and continuum coupling. Applying this framework to @xmath0Sn, we demonstrate that pairing correlations substantially affect low-lying excitation modes, while their influence on giant resonances remains minimal. Our analysis reveals that the impact of pairing correlations on low-lying collective modes exhibits parity dependence. This coordinate space approach provides an effective tool for studying nuclear excitations in open-shell systems where both pairing and continuum effects play crucial roles in determining the collective properties of nuclei.

# Abstract

We report the discovery of broad Wolf-Rayet (WR) emission features in the Multiple Mirror Telescope (MMT) spectrum of the northwest component of I Zw 18, the most metal-poor blue compact dwarf (BCD) galaxy known. Two characteristic broad WR bumps are detected at wavelengths λ≈4650 Å and λ≈5800 Å, indicating the presence of both nitrogen-sequence (WN) and carbon-sequence (WC) Wolf-Rayet stars. From the luminosities of the broad He II λ4686 and C IV λ5808 emission lines, we derive total numbers of 17±4 WN stars and 5±2 WC stars. The derived WR-to-O star number ratio of N(WR)/N(O)≈0.02 is in satisfactory agreement with predictions from massive stellar evolution models incorporating enhanced mass-loss rates. While the WC stars can contribute to the observed nebular He II λ4686 emission, the measured line intensity exceeds model predictions by a factor of several, suggesting that additional sources of hard ionizing radiation (λ<228 Å) are required to explain the observed emission.

# Abstract

We present security proofs for a quantum key distribution (QKD) protocol based on encoding in finite high-dimensional Hilbert spaces. This protocol extends Bennett and Brassard's original two-basis, two-state encoding to a multi-basis, multi-state framework. We analyze the mutual information between legitimate parties and an eavesdropper, along with the error rate, as functions of the Hilbert space dimension. Our analysis considers both optimal incoherent and coherent eavesdropping attacks. We derive upper bounds on the tolerable error rate for the legitimate parties to ensure unconditional security against these eavesdropping strategies. The security thresholds are computed as functions of the dimensionality of the encoding space. Additionally, we incorporate realistic noise models accounting for detector imperfections. Our results demonstrate that high-dimensional encoding can provide enhanced security margins and improved noise tolerance compared to conventional two-dimensional protocols, offering practical advantages for implementing secure quantum communication systems.

# Abstract

We investigate quantum tunneling through an oscillating delta-function barrier by exploiting the system's time periodicity. The time-dependent Schrödinger equation is transformed into an infinite matrix equation, which we solve analytically using Toeplitz matrix techniques to reduce it to a tractable @xmath0 matrix form. Analysis of the frequency-dependent transmission amplitudes reveals a novel characteristic time scale governing the tunneling dynamics, distinct from the Büttiker-Landauer traversal time. We present a detailed comparison and establish the relationship between these two fundamental time scales, providing new insights into time-dependent quantum tunneling phenomena.

# Abstract

We demonstrate a proof-of-principle implementation of hybrid quantum-classical simulation for strongly correlated fermion systems in the thermodynamic limit. Using a two-site dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) framework, we map the Hubbard model onto a self-consistent quantum impurity problem. This approach yields a minimal representation requiring only four qubits to encode the impurity degrees of freedom, supplemented by a single ancilla qubit for measurement operations. The self-consistency loop characteristic of DMFT is handled classically, while the quantum processor solves the impurity problem—a task intractable for classical computers in more complex scenarios. We present a detailed protocol for implementing this hybrid algorithm using superconducting qubit architectures, demonstrating that meaningful simulations of correlated electron systems are achievable with current and near-term quantum hardware. This work establishes a practical pathway toward quantum advantage in condensed matter physics using noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices.

We investigate the full counting statistics (FCS) of charge transport in interferometers for chiral Majorana fermions, focusing on systems with two incoming and two outgoing Dirac fermion channels. For non-interacting systems, the FCS is determined by the scattering matrix relating outgoing to incoming Dirac fermions. We derive explicit expressions for higher-order current correlations in a modified Hanbury Brown-Twiss interferometer configuration. Analysis of the cumulant-generating function reveals a remarkable factorization property: unit-charge transfer processes decompose into two independent half-charge transfer processes, equivalently described as two independent electron-hole conversion processes. Through combined analytical calculations and numerical simulations, we demonstrate that this factorization holds universally for arbitrary scattering matrices, establishing it as a fundamental property independent of specific interferometer geometries. This result provides new insights into fractional charge transport in Majorana-based quantum devices.

We investigate the hadronic matrix elements of local four-quark operators relevant for neutrinoless double beta decay processes in nuclei and hyperons within the MIT bag model framework. These operators induce charge changes of two units (@xmath0) and violate lepton number conservation. Using a low energy effective Lagrangian, we calculate the matrix elements without relying on the standard factorization approximation commonly employed for four-quark operators. As a concrete application, we compute the decay amplitude and transition rate for the process @xmath1, which violates lepton number by @xmath2. We present a detailed comparison between results obtained using the full calculation and those derived from the factorization approach, highlighting the differences and assessing the validity of the approximation. This study provides insights into the hadronic aspects of lepton number violating processes in baryon systems.

# Abstract

We analyze the left-right vector-axialvector correlator using spectral functions from hadronic τ decays measured by ALEPH. By computing low-order spectral moments with appropriately chosen weight functions that suppress duality violations, we extract fundamental QCD chiral symmetry breaking parameters. We estimate systematic uncertainties from quark-hadron duality violations using resonance parametrizations constrained by short-distance operator product expansion requirements. Our pinched-weight analysis yields precise determinations of the effective chiral low-energy constants L₁₀ and C₈₇, which characterize the chiral symmetry breaking pattern, along with dimension-six and dimension-eight condensate contributions in the operator product expansion. The method demonstrates excellent control over non-perturbative effects and provides stringent tests of chiral perturbation theory predictions against experimental data from τ hadronic decays.

# Abstract

We investigate coexisting fluctuations toward multiple ordered states in strongly correlated electronic systems using a non-linear sigma model framework. Motivated by observations in underdoped cuprate superconductors showing simultaneous short-range charge order and superconducting fluctuations, we develop a theoretical description accommodating @xmath0 competing orders. We calculate the transverse thermoelectric transport coefficient in the analytically tractable large-@xmath0 limit, quantifying the contribution of order parameter fluctuations to the Nernst signal. Our findings remain applicable at high temperatures for finite @xmath0 and demonstrate consistency with prior Gaussian superconducting fluctuation models. This work provides a unified framework for understanding how competing orders manifest in thermoelectric transport, offering insights into the complex phase diagrams of cuprate superconductors and other strongly correlated materials exhibiting multiple proximate ordered phases.

# Abstract

Zero forcing is a combinatorial game played on graphs where vertices are colored black with the objective of minimizing "unforced" moves needed to color all vertices. The resulting zero forcing number provides an upper bound for the maximum nullity of matrices associated with the graph. We introduce a novel variation of the zero forcing game designed to bound the maximum nullity of graph-associated matrices having exactly @xmath0 negative eigenvalues. This variant constrains the possible number of positive eigenvalues for such graphs, enabling the construction of lower bounds for a graph's inertia set. Our approach extends classical zero forcing techniques to incorporate spectral information about eigenvalue signs, providing a new tool for studying the relationship between graph structure and matrix properties. This work bridges combinatorial graph theory and linear algebra, offering insights into the inertia characteristics of graph-associated matrices through game-theoretic methods.

# Abstract

We investigate quintessence models with potentials characterized by conditions @xmath0 and @xmath1, focusing on scenarios with nonzero initial field velocity. We develop an analytical approximation describing the temporal evolution of the equation of state parameter @xmath2 for the quintessence field. Our analysis reveals a distinctive two-phase evolutionary pattern: an initial "rapid freezing" epoch where @xmath2 decreases temporally, followed by a "slow thawing" phase during which @xmath2 increases. This behavior demonstrates early-time similarity to constant-@xmath3 models, with significant late-time deviations. The analytical framework successfully reproduces numerical solutions with excellent precision, providing insights into the dynamical evolution of quintessence dark energy. These findings have important implications for distinguishing between different dark energy models through observational constraints on the equation of state evolution.

# Abstract

Nonthermal radiation from astrophysical systems containing relativistic jets and shocks, including gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), active galactic nuclei (AGNs), and microquasars, typically displays characteristic power-law emission spectra. Recent particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations of relativistic electron-ion and electron-positron jets propagating into stationary media demonstrate that particle acceleration occurs primarily in the downstream jet region. In collisionless relativistic shocks, acceleration of particles (electrons, positrons, and ions) results from plasma waves and associated instabilities, particularly the Weibel (filamentation) instability generated in the shock region. These simulations reveal that the Weibel instability generates and amplifies highly non-uniform, small-scale magnetic field structures. Such turbulent fields cause transverse deflection of electrons in the post-shock region, producing "jitter" radiation with properties fundamentally different from standard synchrotron radiation, which assumes uniform magnetic fields. We propose that jitter radiation may provide crucial insights into the complex temporal evolution and spectral features observed in gamma-ray bursts, relativistic jets, and supernova remnants, offering an alternative interpretation to conventional synchrotron models.

# Abstract

This paper presents a characterization of compact subsets of the fuzzy number space equipped with the level convergence topology. Based on this characterization, we establish that compactness is equivalent to sequential compactness in the fuzzy number space under the level convergence topology. 

Diamond and Kloeden previously provided a characterization of compact sets in fuzzy number spaces equipped with the supremum metric, while Fang and Xue offered a characterization for one-dimensional fuzzy number spaces with the supremum metric, the latter being a special case of the former. However, we identify a fundamental conflict between our characterization and those presented by these authors. Through a counterexample, we demonstrate that the characterizations given by Diamond-Kloeden and Fang-Xue are incorrect.

Our results provide a corrected understanding of compactness in fuzzy number spaces and clarify the relationship between different topological structures on these spaces, particularly concerning the level convergence topology and supremum metric.

**Keywords:** fuzzy numbers; supremum metric; level convergence; compactness; sequential compactness

# Abstract

We investigate the stationary state solutions of a bond-diluted kinetic Ising model subjected to a time-dependent oscillating magnetic field on a honeycomb lattice using effective-field theory (EFT). The system's temporal evolution is described through a master equation formalism. Our analysis focuses on how bond dilution, along with the external field's frequency @xmath1 and amplitude @xmath2, influences dynamic phase diagrams. 

We demonstrate that the system undergoes first-order phase transitions characterized by a dynamic tricritical point (DTCP) in low-temperature, high-amplitude regimes, contrasting with previous findings for undiluted systems. Bond dilution introduces several novel phenomena, including reentrant behavior, and systematically suppresses first-order transitions and the DTCP. These effects reflect the competing influences of thermal fluctuations, disorder-induced frustration, and time-dependent driving forces.

Additionally, we examine how the bond percolation threshold varies with the oscillating field's amplitude and frequency, revealing intricate interplay between structural disorder and dynamic ordering. Our results provide insights into the role of quenched disorder in driven magnetic systems and contribute to understanding non-equilibrium phase transitions in diluted lattice models with applications to disordered magnetic materials and related systems.

# Abstract

We present results from the second phase of the Super-Kamiokande solar neutrino measurement and compare them with first-phase observations. The solar neutrino flux spectrum, temporal variations, and oscillation parameters demonstrate statistical consistency across both phases, with no evidence of spectral distortion. Combined data from phases I and II span the complete solar cycle 23, revealing no correlation between neutrino flux and solar activity. The measured @xmath0B total flux is determined to be @xmath1, while the day-night asymmetry yields @xmath2. Our analysis reveals no systematic differences between the two experimental phases, strengthening confidence in the detector's long-term stability and the robustness of solar neutrino measurements. These results provide important constraints on neutrino oscillation parameters and confirm the MSW effect predictions for solar neutrinos traversing Earth.

We investigate non-LTE (NLTE) effects for magnesium and calcium in the atmospheres of late-type giant and supergiant stars. The aim of this paper is to provide a comprehensive grid of NLTE/LTE equivalent width ratios for Mg and Ca lines covering a wide range of stellar parameters: effective temperatures @xmath1 K, surface gravities @xmath2 dex, and metallicities [Fe/H] @xmath3 ∈ [-4.0, 0.5] dex. We employ realistic model atoms incorporating state-of-the-art atomic physics and fine structure effects. Our analysis focuses on Mg and Ca lines in the optical and near-infrared spectral regions, with particular emphasis on lines within the _Gaia_ Radial Velocity Spectrograph (RVS) wavelength domain [8470, 8740] Å. The computed NLTE corrections are presented both as tabulated functions of stellar parameters in electronic format and as polynomial fits specifically for the _Gaia_/RVS lines. These corrections are essential for accurate abundance determinations and will facilitate the interpretation of large-scale spectroscopic surveys of evolved stars in the Galaxy.

We present a generalization of Landauer-Büttiker theory for networks of interacting metallic carbon nanotubes. Beginning with symmetric starlike junctions, we extend our approach to asymmetric systems. The symmetric case admits closed-form solutions, while asymmetric configurations require combined perturbative and non-perturbative methods. For @xmath0 repulsively interacting nanotubes, the symmetric system's only stable fixed point represents an isolated node. We provide detailed results for both symmetric and asymmetric systems at @xmath1, corresponding to carbon nanotube Y junctions. This framework enables systematic analysis of interaction effects in nanotube network geometries, revealing the role of symmetry in determining transport properties.

This letter presents an optimal discriminant function framework for modulation classification utilizing sampled distribution distance metrics. The proposed low-complexity approach classifies candidate signal constellations by measuring distribution distances at strategically selected testpoints along the cumulative distribution function. Employing Bayesian decision criteria, the method asymptotically achieves minimum classification error for a given testpoint set. Performance is further enhanced through testpoint location optimization. Simulation results demonstrate substantial improvements over existing distribution-based classification techniques, offering superior accuracy while maintaining computational efficiency in distinguishing various modulation schemes.

# Abstract

This paper addresses boundary stabilization of a cascade ODE-heat system with state delay under actuator saturation constraints. A state feedback controller is designed using the backstepping method to achieve system stabilization. The domain of attraction is characterized through Lyapunov-based analysis, providing explicit bounds on initial conditions guaranteeing stability. Exponential stability of the delayed cascaded system is rigorously established using Halanay's inequality, which handles the time-delay effects. The saturation nonlinearity is incorporated into the controller design to ensure practical implementability. Numerical simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, validating theoretical results and illustrating convergence properties within the estimated domain of attraction for various initial conditions and delay parameters.

# Abstract

Quantum link models provide an alternative non-perturbative formulation of abelian and non-abelian lattice gauge theories. They are ideally suited for quantum simulation, for example, using ultracold atoms in an optical lattice. This holds the promise to address currently unsolvable problems, such as the real-time and high-density dynamics of strongly interacting matter, first in toy-model gauge theories, and ultimately in QCD. Unlike traditional lattice gauge theory with continuous gauge fields, quantum link models employ discrete quantum degrees of freedom on links, making them naturally compatible with quantum computing architectures. This approach circumvents the sign problem that plagues Monte Carlo simulations at finite density and enables direct investigation of real-time dynamics.

# Abstract

We investigate the nonlinear dynamics of series arrays of Josephson junctions in the large-@xmath0 limit, where @xmath0 represents the number of junctions in the array. The system under consideration consists of identical, overdamped Josephson junctions driven by a constant bias current and globally coupled through a common load impedance. Previous numerical simulations of such arrays have revealed surprisingly simple dynamical behavior, suggesting the existence of hidden symmetries or other underlying mathematical structures that constrain the system's evolution. These intriguing observations were subsequently explained through the discovery of @xmath1 constants of motion, which confine the system's trajectories in phase space to low-dimensional invariant manifolds.

In this work, we demonstrate that the effective dimensionality of the system can be reduced even further by focusing on a special family of states recently identified by Ott and Antonsen in their studies of large populations of coupled oscillators. In geometric terms, the Ott-Antonsen ansatz corresponds to an invariant submanifold whose dimension is one less than that of the manifolds found in earlier investigations. This additional reduction yields significant analytical tractability while capturing the essential dynamics of the system.

We derive the governing equations for the flow on this reduced submanifold and provide detailed analysis for two physically important special cases: arrays with purely resistive loading and arrays with resistive-inductive-capacitive (RLC) loading. For both cases, we obtain analytical or semi-analytical results that characterize the stability, bifurcations, and long-time behavior of the coupled junction arrays.

Our results successfully recover previous findings that were based on linearization arguments and perturbative analyses, while in some instances providing improvements and extensions. Specifically, we obtain exact results in parameter regimes where earlier approximations were necessary, and we identify new dynamical features that were not accessible through previous methods.

The mathematical framework developed here provides new insights into the collective behavior of Josephson junction arrays and demonstrates the power of the Ott-Antonsen reduction technique in systems with global coupling. From a practical perspective, understanding these simplified dynamics is crucial for optimizing the performance of Josephson junction arrays in applications such as voltage standards, oscillators, and detectors. More broadly, our work contributes to the general understanding of how complexity can emerge from, or be suppressed by, the collective dynamics of many coupled nonlinear oscillators, with potential applications extending beyond superconducting devices to other coupled oscillator systems in physics, biology, and engineering.

# Abstract

We present a comprehensive analysis of the electromagnetic self-energy and self-force acting on a scalar point-like charged test particle at rest in the spacetime of a global monopole with general spherically symmetric internal structure. The investigation is carried out by constructing the three-dimensional Green function appropriate for this physical configuration. Our results demonstrate that for observation points exterior to the monopole's core, the scalar self-energy decomposes into two distinct contributions: the first arises from the non-trivial topological structure of the global monopole treated as a point defect, while the second represents a correction term attributable to its finite internal structure. For interior points, the self-energy maintains a similar decomposition, though the primary contribution now depends explicitly on the internal spacetime geometry. To illustrate our general formalism, we examine two specific models for the monopole's interior region: the "flower-pot" and "ballpoint-pen" configurations. For both scenarios, we derive exact analytical expressions for the self-energies and self-forces in both the exterior and interior regions of the global monopole. These results provide insight into how the internal structure of topological defects affects quantum field theoretical quantities and may have implications for particle physics phenomenology in curved spacetimes containing such defects.

# Abstract

Accretion disks around black holes are fundamental systems for understanding matter inflow and energy release in extreme gravitational environments. Magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence drives the angular momentum transport that enables accretion. Recent global general relativistic MHD simulations have provided unprecedented quantitative insights into this process, revealing several previously unrecognized phenomena. These include unexpectedly strong magnetic stresses operating in the marginally stable and plunging regions immediately surrounding the black hole event horizon, and the spontaneous formation of electromagnetically-dominated conical relativistic jets emerging directly from the accretion flow without requiring large-scale magnetic fields. The energy release mechanisms associated with both enhanced near-horizon stresses and jet formation can substantially exceed classical predictions derived from purely hydrodynamic models, with important implications for observed high-energy emission from accreting black holes across the mass spectrum.

# Abstract

We present a kinematic analysis of 75 star-forming galaxies at z~2 in the COSMOS legacy field using near-infrared spectroscopy from Keck/MOSFIRE as part of the ZFIRE survey. Our Ks-band selected sample from the ZFOURGE survey spans stellar masses of log(M*/M☉)~9-11, including 28 galaxies in a known overdensity at z=2.095. We measure Hα emission-line integrated velocity dispersions ranging from 50-230 km s⁻¹, consistent with previous studies of z~2 field galaxies. Using these measurements, we estimate virial, stellar, and gas masses and examine correlations between these properties for both cluster and field populations. Our analysis indicates that baryons dominate the mass budget within the central effective radius. Importantly, we find no statistically significant kinematic differences between cluster and field star-forming galaxies at z~2. This suggests that environmental effects on galaxy kinematics are not yet prominent at this epoch, and that the distinct kinematic properties observed in lower-redshift cluster galaxies develop at later times. These results provide important constraints on the timescales of environmental processing in galaxy clusters.

We investigate the electronic structure of Cr@xmath0NbSe@xmath1 through optical spectroscopy measurements. In the paramagnetic phase, two distinct low-energy interband transitions are identified. Upon entering the ferromagnetic state below the Curie temperature, these transitions split into four peaks. Band structure calculations reveal these peaks correspond to interband transitions involving spin-up Cr e@xmath2 states. Contrary to conventional expectations, we demonstrate that the observed peak splitting is not caused by exchange splitting between spin-up and spin-down bands. Instead, it directly manifests a band broadening effect in Cr-derived electronic states that occurs during spontaneous ferromagnetic ordering, providing new insights into the magnetic transition mechanism.

# Abstract

We investigate the skinning map, a fundamental self-map of Teichmüller space arising from hyperbolic 3-manifolds with boundary. Our focus is on a specific 3-manifold @xmath0—a genus-2 handlebody with two rank-1 cusps. By exploiting an orientation-reversing isometry of @xmath0, we prove that the associated skinning map fixes a particular path in Teichmüller space. Through extremal length estimates, we establish the non-monotonic behavior of this map along the fixed path and demonstrate the existence of critical points. Furthermore, we construct a family of finite covers of @xmath0 that yields examples of skinning maps failing to be immersions on Teichmüller spaces of surfaces with arbitrary even genus and either @xmath1 or @xmath2 punctures. # Abstract

We present the first measurements of europium isotope fractions in s-process-enhanced, metal-poor stars, providing direct observational constraints on the @xmath0Sm branching point in s-process nucleosynthesis. High-resolution spectroscopy of two carbon-rich, very metal-poor stars (LP 62544 and CS 31062050) was obtained with the Subaru Telescope High Dispersion Spectrograph. Through detailed analysis of spectral lines affected by hyperfine splitting and isotope shifts, we derive @xmath0Eu fractions of 0.60±@xmath2 and 0.55±@xmath2 for LP 62544 and CS 31062050, respectively. These values significantly exceed the solar-system ratio, demonstrating different s-process conditions in the early Galaxy. The elevated @xmath0Eu fractions agree well with predictions from recent pulsed s-process models in asymptotic giant branch stars. Using these measurements in conjunction with theoretical calculations, we derive new constraints on the neutron density and temperature conditions during s-process nucleosynthesis at low metallicity. # Abstract

October 2004 marks the 400th anniversary of the sighting of SN 1604, now marked by the presence of an expanding nebulosity known as Kepler's supernova remnant. Of the small number of remnants of historical supernovae, Kepler's remnant remains the most enigmatic. The supernova type, and hence the type of star that exploded, is still a matter of debate, and even the distance to the remnant is uncertain by more than a factor of two. As new and improved multiwavelength observations become available, and as the time baseline of observations gets longer, Kepler's supernova remnant is slowly revealing its secrets. This review examines recent and current observations of Kepler's supernova remnant across the electromagnetic spectrum, from radio to X-ray wavelengths, and discusses what these observations indicate about the nature of this intriguing object. Progress in understanding the progenitor system, explosion mechanism, and interaction with the surrounding interstellar medium is evaluated, highlighting remaining questions and future observational prospects.

# Abstract

We present comprehensive data reduction algorithms developed for the Multiband Imaging Photometer for Spitzer (MIPS) instrument, drawing upon extensive preflight testing, modeling, and refinement through initial flight observations. The MIPS focal planes consist of Si:As detectors (24 μm) and Ge:Ga detectors (70 and 160 μm), representative of advanced infrared detector arrays operating in the low-background space environment. 

The Ge:Ga bulk photoconductor arrays exhibit various systematic artifacts requiring careful correction for accurate photometric calibration, while the Si:As array, though more stable, also demonstrates specific instrumental effects necessitating removal. Our data reduction pipeline comprises three sequential stages: (1) conversion of non-destructive readout ramps into flux slopes while correcting artifacts with time constants comparable to individual exposure durations; (2) calibration of slope measurements addressing longer-timescale artifacts; and (3) iterative refinement exploiting observational redundancy inherent in MIPS scanning modes to enhance artifact removal.

For each processing stage, we provide detailed descriptions of the underlying physics informed by laboratory characterization experiments and theoretical frameworks, accompanied by the mathematical formulations implemented in the calibration algorithms. We demonstrate the efficacy of these approaches through comparison of preflight predictions with actual on-orbit performance. These reduction techniques are broadly applicable to similar infrared detector systems and provide valuable insights into the systematic behaviors characteristic of space-based photoconductor arrays. The algorithms successfully mitigate instrumental signatures, enabling precise photometric measurements essential for MIPS science objectives.

# Abstract

We investigate correlation-driven orbital Mott transitions in two-dimensional pyrochlore lattices through a model Hamiltonian incorporating Hund's coupling between itinerant and localized electrons alongside Coulomb interactions. In the weak coupling regime, zero-temperature susceptibility calculations within the random phase approximation reveal a para-orbital phase. For strong coupling, we employ Green's function perturbation theory to derive an effective Hamiltonian, demonstrating ferro-orbital ordering at zero temperature. To map the complete phase diagram, we implement static auxiliary field Monte Carlo simulations that explicitly preserve spatial correlations, enabling systematic exploration of finite-temperature behavior. Our results elucidate the interplay between electronic correlations and orbital degrees of freedom in geometrically frustrated lattices, revealing distinct orbital ordering transitions driven by interaction strength and temperature variations in this frustrated magnetic system.

# Abstract

We investigate the origin of quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) observed in accreting neutron star systems by examining global hydrodynamic modes in the boundary layer between the accretion disk and the neutron star magnetosphere. The observational characteristics of these QPOs suggest that oscillatory modes in the innermost disk regions are responsible for the observed signals. In particular, very high frequency modes associated with the radial epicyclic frequency @xmath0 can exist in these inner regions. Unlike in purely Keplerian disks where @xmath1 is degenerate with the orbital frequency @xmath2, this degeneracy is lifted in the non-Keplerian transition zone near the magnetopause.

Through analysis of long-wavelength global hydrodynamic modes in viscous accretion disk boundary layers, we demonstrate that the fastest growing mode frequencies cluster in bands centered around @xmath0 and @xmath3. These modes achieve maximum growth rates near the radius where @xmath2 reaches its maximum value. The specific modes that become unstable at any given radius depend on global hydrodynamic parameters including the surface density profile and radial drift velocity.

Significantly, our model naturally explains a key observational feature of kilohertz QPOs in neutron star systems: the frequency separation between consecutive bands of the fastest growing modes equals the neutron star spin frequency. This result emerges directly from the boundary conditions imposed by the rotating magnetosphere on the inner disk, providing strong theoretical support for the connection between QPO phenomena and disk-magnetosphere interactions.

# Abstract

We demonstrate deterministic coupling between single semiconductor nanowire quantum dots with visible emission and plasmonic gold nanoantennas. Prior to integration, both components undergo comprehensive characterization via microphotoluminescence and cathodoluminescence spectroscopy. A novel two-step cathodoluminescence-based realignment procedure enables precise electron beam lithography positioning of Au antennas adjacent to individual nanowire quantum dots with nanometer-scale accuracy. Systematic optical measurements performed before and after antenna fabrication reveal significant modifications to the hybrid system's photophysical properties. Specifically, we observe enhanced nanowire absorption cross-sections and accelerated quantum dot spontaneous emission rates, with enhancement factors reaching twofold in optimally coupled antenna-quantum dot configurations. These results establish a reliable fabrication methodology for integrating semiconductor nanostructures with plasmonic elements, advancing prospects for quantum nanophotonic devices operating in the visible spectrum.

# Abstract

We investigate the influence of a primordial background magnetic field, consistent with current observational bounds, on the linear evolution of cosmological density perturbations at sub-Hubble scales. The magnetic field introduces anisotropic pressure support that modifies gravitational collapse, with magnetic pressure acting exclusively in the plane perpendicular to the field direction. This anisotropy leads to a direction-dependent "Jeans length," causing perturbations to evolve non-spherically. We establish this behavior through analytical derivation and confirm it via numerical integration of ideal magnetohydrodynamic equations during the matter-dominated epoch.

Our analysis reveals distinct evolutionary phases: prior to recombination, thermal pressure dominates and perturbations follow standard growth patterns, while post-recombination dynamics are governed by magnetic pressure, producing pronounced anisotropic evolution. We quantify this anisotropy by calculating the eccentricity of initially spherical Gaussian perturbations in coordinate space. For sub-galactic scale fluctuations with background magnetic field strength of order @xmath3 Gauss—compatible with observational constraints—we find eccentricities @xmath0 reaching @xmath1 by redshift @xmath2. These results demonstrate that even weak primordial magnetic fields can significantly impact structure formation geometry, with implications for understanding the morphology of early cosmic structures and placing constraints on primordial magnetogenesis scenarios through observations of small-scale matter distribution.

# Abstract

Within the framework of the standard fireball model, GRBs originate from synchrotron radiation and Compton scattering in ultra-relativistic jets emanating from central engines. The prevailing interpretation attributes prompt emission to internal shocks arising from collisions between shells of varying velocities, where the magnetic field advected from the central engine maintains large-scale order. Conversely, afterglow emission results from external shocks produced when the jet interacts with the interstellar medium, generating potentially random magnetic fields through mechanisms such as Weibel instability.

This study presents detailed calculations of polarization properties for synchrotron self-Compton processes in highly relativistic jets characterized by randomly distributed magnetic fields within the shock plane. We extend our analysis to encompass configurations where a uniform magnetic component perpendicular to the shock plane is superimposed on the random component. Our results demonstrate that polarization levels exceeding @xmath1 are difficult to achieve when seed electrons exhibit isotropic distributions in the jet frame. This theoretical constraint provides a natural explanation for the observed polarization upper limits during GRB afterglow phases.

Furthermore, we investigate scenarios involving differential temporal decay rates between random and uniform magnetic field components. Our analysis reveals that such evolution can induce @xmath2 rotations in the polarization angle over time. These findings offer important insights into the magnetic field structure and evolution in GRB jets, with implications for interpreting current and future polarimetric observations of these energetic cosmic phenomena.

# Abstract

We report results from a systematic search for arcminute-scale anisotropy in the cosmic microwave background (CMB) using the Berkeley-Illinois-Maryland-Association (BIMA) array equipped with sensitive centimeter-wave receivers. Our observations probe CMB angular power on scales corresponding to multipole @xmath1 (approximately @xmath2 angular scale), where secondary anisotropies and primordial fluctuations are expected to contribute significantly.

Employing a Bayesian analysis framework applied directly to interferometric visibility data, we detect CMB anisotropy with flat-band power @xmath4K at @xmath5 confidence level. The statistical significance of a non-zero detection is @xmath6, with an upper limit of @xmath7K at @xmath8 confidence.

To assess potential contamination from discrete radio sources, we conducted concurrent observations at 4.8 GHz using the Very Large Array (VLA). Our analysis demonstrates that point source contributions to the measured anisotropy are negligible. We establish fundamental connections between cyclic presentations of groups and cyclic branched coverings of @xmath0-knots. This framework provides a combinatorial approach to understanding the topology of branched coverings through group presentations, linking knot theory with geometric group theory. The cyclic structure inherent in both the covering space and the group presentation reveals deep algebraic-topological relationships in low-dimensional topology.

# Abstract

We establish a sufficient condition for finite-time wave breaking in strong solutions to the Camassa-Holm equation, based on the decay rate of initial data at infinity. We prove that solutions undergo wave breaking when initial data decay faster than soliton solutions. Conversely, for initial data with slower decay than solitons, we demonstrate persistence results in weighted @xmath0-spaces for a broad class of moderate weights. The threshold between blow-up and persistence is precisely characterized by the soliton decay rate. We provide explicit asymptotic profiles that demonstrate the optimality of our conditions, revealing a sharp dichotomy between global existence and finite-time singularity formation based on tail behavior of initial data.

# Abstract

Fundamental principles in quantum optics dictate that deterministic linear amplification of quantum states inevitably introduces noise, degrading pure states into mixed states. Recent advances have demonstrated that probabilistic, non-deterministic amplifiers can circumvent this limitation, enabling noiseless amplification. We present a novel noiseless amplification scheme that exploits the intrinsic stochastic fluctuations of the quantum field itself as the energy source for amplification, eliminating the need for external energy injection. This approach fundamentally differs from conventional amplification schemes. We analyze the trade-off between amplification gain and success probability, characterizing the statistical properties of output states for both successful and unsuccessful amplification attempts. Through optimization of beam splitter reflectivities, we determine the maximum achievable success rates and establish the operational parameter space. Our analysis reveals the relationship between this fluctuation-driven amplification mechanism and previously proposed noiseless amplification protocols, providing insights into the fundamental limits and practical implementations of probabilistic quantum amplification. This work advances our understanding of energy redistribution in quantum optical systems and offers new perspectives for quantum information processing applications.

# Abstract

We investigate the emergence of symmetry restoration in highly excited hadronic states through semiclassical analysis. In quantum chromodynamics (QCD), systems with large radial quantum number @xmath0 or high angular momentum enter the semiclassical (WKB) regime where quantum fluctuations become suppressed. Since both chiral symmetry breaking and @xmath1 symmetry breaking originate from quantum effects, these symmetry violations must diminish asymptotically in the high-energy spectrum. Consequently, highly-excited hadrons should manifest the @xmath2 symmetry inherent in the classical QCD Lagrangian. 

This argument gains additional strength in the large-@xmath3 limit for mesons, where all mesonic states become stable against strong decays, yielding an infinite spectrum. In this regime, mesons of arbitrarily large spatial extent and action can be excited, making the semiclassical approximation rigorous. Importantly, the exact @xmath4 limit is unnecessary—for any sufficiently large action, there exists a corresponding @xmath3 value for which isolated mesons exist and admit semiclassical description.

# Abstract

We investigate the physical mechanisms governing the low-redshift Lyα forest using hydrodynamic simulations of four cold dark matter cosmological models. While our primary conclusions are robust across different cosmologies, they critically depend on our modeling of a declining UV ionizing background that tracks the decreasing quasar population at low redshift.

Our analysis reveals that cosmic expansion drives rapid evolution in the line number density dn/dz (counting absorbers above a specified equivalent width threshold) at z > 1.5. However, at lower redshifts, the fading UV background counterbalances expansion effects, resulting in remarkably slow evolution of dn/dz. The gravitational infall of gas from low-density regions into collapsed structures produces a modest but measurable impact on dn/dz evolution, particularly for high equivalent width systems.

At all redshifts, we find a systematic relationship between line strength and physical origin: weak absorbers predominantly trace moderate density fluctuations in the diffuse, unshocked intergalactic medium (IGM), while stronger systems arise in shocked or radiatively cooled gas at higher overdensities. However, cosmic expansion causes the neutral hydrogen column density of structures at fixed overdensity to decline with time. Consequently, absorbers at z ~ 0 are dynamically analogous to systems with 10-50 times higher column densities at z ~ 3. The mildly overdense IGM fluctuations responsible for most forest opacity at z ~ 3 produce only optically thin lines at z ~ 0, whereas marginally saturated lines (NHI ~ 10^14 cm^-2) at low redshift typically originate in gas overdense by factors of ~5-10.

We observe no sharp boundary between absorption arising in "galaxy halos" versus large-scale structures; rather, galaxies preferentially inhabit dense IGM regions that produce strong Lyα lines. This continuous distribution naturally explains key observational characteristics of the low-redshift forest: (1) the pronounced transition in dn/dz evolution near z ~ 1, (2) stronger evolutionary trends for higher equivalent width absorbers, (3) an extended correlation between Lyα equivalent width and galaxy impact parameter reaching ~1 h^-1 Mpc, and (4) the association of strong lines with galaxy environments while weak lines trace more diffuse cosmic structure. Our simulations thus provide a coherent physical framework unifying the distinctive observed properties of low-redshift Lyα absorption systems.

# Abstract

This paper investigates the fundamental memory-transmission-rate tradeoff in caching systems using a novel computer-aided approach that departs from conventional analytical methods in information theory. We leverage linear programming (LP) characterizations of the entropy space as our foundation, but extend significantly beyond traditional information inequality proofs.

Our methodology begins by identifying and formalizing the inherent symmetry structure in caching problems, which allows us to establish the existence of optimal symmetric solutions. Through symmetry reduction techniques, we develop tractable linear programs that identify the boundary of the memory-transmission-rate tradeoff region for several fundamental cases, yielding tight outer bounds. These computational results serve as the basis for formulating general hypotheses about the optimal tradeoff region, which we subsequently prove analytically. This approach yields a complete characterization of the optimal tradeoff for two-user systems and partial characterizations for two-file systems.

A key contribution is our reverse-engineering methodology: by carefully analyzing the joint entropy structure revealed by outer bounds in specific cases, we derive novel code constructions that generalize to a broader class of achievable schemes. This demonstrates how computational insights can guide practical coding strategies.

Furthermore, we develop techniques for computing strong outer bounds through strategic relaxation of the LP formulation. This approach provides two significant benefits: (1) it enables us to deduce generic characteristics of converse proofs, revealing common structural elements across different problem instances, and (2) it makes computation tractable for larger problem instances that would otherwise be computationally infeasible.

Our work demonstrates the power of combining computational and analytical techniques in information theory, establishing a framework for computer-aided analysis that can accelerate progress on fundamental problems in network information theory and coded caching.

We investigate statistical properties of random walks on experimental crumpled wire configurations rigidly jammed in two dimensions. These hierarchical structures with complex topology result from metallic wire injection at constant rate into a transparent planar cell of diameter @xmath0. The observed diffusion exhibits anomalous behavior with an exponent closely matching that of two-dimensional percolation threshold. We compare our system with other physically relevant systems and discuss experimental implications. The crumpled wire provides a novel experimental realization for studying anomalous transport in disordered media with intricate geometrical and topological properties.

# Abstract

First-order Fermi acceleration at astrophysical shocks represents a fundamental mechanism for generating non-thermal particle populations in various cosmic environments. While the test-particle approximation provides a simplified framework where accelerated particles negligibly influence the shock structure, realistic scenarios often require consideration of particle backreaction on the fluid dynamics. This backreaction introduces the non-linear regime of shock acceleration, characterized by significant modifications to both shock structure and particle spectra. We present a semi-analytical methodology for treating non-linear effects in diffusive shock acceleration, examining how energetic particle pressure affects the compression ratio, precursor formation, and spectral steepening. Our approach is validated through systematic comparisons with previous theoretical treatments and state-of-the-art numerical simulations, demonstrating improved consistency in predicting maximum particle energies and acceleration efficiencies in strongly modified shocks relevant to supernova remnants and other high-energy astrophysical sources.

# Abstract

Preliminary measurements include the left-right asymmetry @xmath1 and leptonic final state asymmetries @xmath2, @xmath3, and @xmath4. These results are combined to extract a preliminary value of the effective weak mixing angle: @xmath5. Additionally, we report direct measurements of @xmath6 using left-right forward-backward asymmetries from partial data samples spanning 1993-1998. The preliminary @xmath6 determination combines results from jet charge, cascade kaon tag, and semileptonic decay analyses, yielding @xmath7. # Abstract

We present a comprehensive diagnostic framework for investigating gamma-ray emission lines from radioactive isotopes, specifically ²⁶Al and ⁶⁰Fe, in galactic stellar clusters and associations through multi-wavelength analysis. Our evolutionary synthesis models build upon previous work, incorporating state-of-the-art stellar evolution tracks, updated stellar atmospheres for OB and Wolf-Rayet (WR) stars, and refined nucleosynthetic yields from massive stars during both hydrostatic burning and explosive supernova events (Type II and Type Ib).

For coeval stellar populations, we trace the temporal evolution of ²⁶Al and ⁶⁰Fe production, calculating the equivalent ²⁶Al yield per ionizing O7V star and other observable quantities. Our analysis reveals four distinct phases in the 1.809 MeV ²⁶Al emission line: (1) a stellar wind-dominated phase lasting approximately 0-3 Myr, (2) a SN Ib-dominated phase from 3-7 Myr, (3) a SN II-dominated phase extending from 7-37 Myr, and (4) an exponential decay phase beyond 37 Myr. The equivalent ²⁶Al yield emerges as an exceptionally sensitive age indicator, enabling differentiation between Wolf-Rayet and supernova nucleosynthesis contributions within stellar associations. Additionally, the ²⁶Al/⁶⁰Fe emissivity ratio serves as an independent age constraint that quantifies the relative importance of explosive nucleosynthesis.

Applying our models to solar metallicity populations at steady state, we determine the fractional contributions to ²⁶Al production: approximately 30% from pre-WR phase stars, 30% from WR stars, 25% from SN Ib events, and 15% from SN II explosions. For ⁶⁰Fe, we find that 20% originates from SN Ib while 80% comes from SN II. Normalizing to the Galaxy's total ionizing flux, we predict production rates of 1.5 M⊙ Myr⁻¹ for ²⁶Al and 0.8 M⊙ Myr⁻¹ for ⁶⁰Fe, corresponding to present-day interstellar medium masses of 1.5 M⊙ and 1.7 M⊙, respectively.

To facilitate rigorous quantitative analysis of observational data, we develop a Bayesian statistical framework that properly accounts for initial mass function stochasticity and observational uncertainties. We implement Monte Carlo techniques to generate probability distributions for all relevant observables, providing a robust methodology for comparing theoretical predictions with measurements. We demonstrate this approach through application to a hypothetical massive stellar association, establishing the foundation for detailed analyses. Forthcoming companion papers will present applications to observed regions including Cygnus and Vela, demonstrating the diagnostic power of this integrated multi-wavelength approach.

# Abstract

We investigate time-independent, radially symmetric BPS soliton solutions in a @xmath0 model coupled to an Abelian gauge field with standard Maxwell dynamics. A consistent self-dual framework is constructed, establishing a well-defined lower bound for the system's energy. This bound is saturated by solutions satisfying a specific set of coupled first-order BPS differential equations. Using appropriate boundary conditions, we obtain numerical solutions corresponding to regular, finite-energy configurations. The main characteristics of these solitonic structures are discussed in detail. Notably, we examine different solution branches corresponding to distinct choices of an auxiliary function @xmath1 that parameterizes the model. Despite the apparent differences between these branches, we demonstrate that all resulting scenarios exhibit identical phenomenology and are physically equivalent. This equivalence suggests a robust underlying structure in the self-dual formulation, independent of the particular representation chosen for the auxiliary function, thus unifying seemingly disparate solution classes within a single physical framework.

# Abstract

Two-dimensional angular correlations from 200 GeV Au+Au collisions reveal a same-side (SS) peak at azimuth $\Delta\phi \approx 0$ that exhibits characteristics consistent with jet formation in peripheral collisions. As collision centrality increases, this SS peak undergoes systematic modifications: it becomes elongated along pseudorapidity $\Delta\eta$ and shows altered transverse momentum $p_t$ structure. This elongated feature, termed the "soft ridge," has been interpreted as evidence for collective flow phenomena, including triangular and higher harmonic flows potentially connected to initial-state geometry. This work establishes the connection between so-called "higher harmonic flows" and SS 2D peak properties. A comprehensive analysis of the SS peak across all centralities supports a consistent jet-based interpretation, challenging flow-based explanations and providing an alternative framework for understanding these correlation structures in heavy-ion collisions.

# Abstract

We investigate vector soliton emission from two-component elongated Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs) through temporal manipulation of inter- and intra-species scattering lengths via Feshbach resonance tuning. Our study reveals phenomena unique to multi-component systems without single-species analogues. We demonstrate vector soliton out-coupling through interspecies interaction tuning, show how one species' evolution can be controlled by modulating the dynamics of the other, and present implementations of supersolitons. The analysis employs numerical simulations of the one-dimensional coupled Gross-Pitaevskii equations, complemented by analytical arguments providing qualitative physical insight. These results establish novel control mechanisms for matter-wave engineering in binary condensates, exploiting the rich interplay between components through time-dependent scattering length manipulation. Our findings open new avenues for coherent atom optics and nonlinear wave management in multi-component quantum gases.

# Abstract

We present a comprehensive study of super giant molecular complexes (SGMCs) in the merging galaxy system NGC 4038/39 (the Antennae) using previously published CO emission observations to investigate the formation mechanisms of young massive star clusters.
